title: Nickeson v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Judicial Scrutiny of Innovation: A Definitive Analysis of Nickeson v. Commissioner and the Evolving Standards for Research and Development Tax Incentives
court: United States Court of Appeals, Tenth Circuit
subject: Profit Motive and Trade or Business in R&D Tax Shelters
summary: Nickeson v. Commissioner, 962 F.2d 973 (10th Cir. 1992), is a key federal precedent shaping R&D tax deductions and the research credit in the United States. It holds that taxpayers claiming IRC § 174 research expenses must prove both a genuine profit motive and substantial, regular, active involvement in a trade or business—passive investors in promoted tax shelters cannot qualify.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

In Nickeson v. Commissioner, 962 F.2d 973 (10th Cir. 1992), affirming Brock v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1989-641, 58 T.C.M. (CCH) 826 (1989), the United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit established a foundational judicial framework for distinguishing legitimate research and development (R&D) ventures from abusive tax shelters. The ruling addresses the threshold statutory requirements under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174 for deducting or amortizing research or experimental (R&E) expenditures, which simultaneously serve as the primary statutory gateway for claiming the federal Research and Development Tax Credit under IRC § 41. By identifying five objective characteristics that courts rely on in rejecting deductions for lack of profit motive, and by requiring taxpayers to show both a profit motive and activities "substantial and regular enough" to establish active involvement in order to satisfy the "in connection with [a] trade or business" requirement, the Tenth Circuit reinforced the limits on § 174 deductions claimed through promoted R&D tax-shelter arrangements.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Factual Context

The litigation originated from the United States Tax Court decision reported as Brock v. Commissioner, 58 T.C.M. (CCH) 826 (1989), involving individual taxpayers—including appellants Daniel B. and Enid C. Nickeson and Norman E. and Nancy J. Kuhl—who claimed deductions for research and development expenses under IRC § 174 on their 1982 federal income tax returns. The taxpayers purchased individual aspects or components of an automatic meter reading device (AMR) through a program promoted by George Risk, an inventor and the principal of several corporations, including George Risk Industries, Inc. (GRI) and G.R.I. Research and Development Laboratories (R & D Labs), the promoter-affiliated entity to which the deferred payments were owed; Risk held only a nonexclusive license, without the right to sublicense, to use eleven aspects of a patent on AMR improvements owned by Harris Corporation.

Structurally, the venture followed the promoted tax-shelter model prevalent during the early 1980s. Beginning in 1981, Risk sold the AMR components for a specified price payable 25% in cash, with the remainder due in deferred promissory notes payable to R & D Labs; the notes, which constituted 75% of the purchase price, were payable from and secured by the proceeds of exploiting the research information and were nonrecourse in substance. The purchase agreements gave the taxpayers the right to technological information concerning the component purchased (or possibly the AMR as a whole), which ostensibly they could use to manufacture and sell their component or sell to a licensee corporation created as part of the AMR project, but the agreements did not describe the research needed, set a time frame for it, provide for accounting to the taxpayers on progress or expenditures, or transfer ownership rights in the underlying technology. The taxpayers' claimed deductions equalled the cash actually paid plus the face amount of the promissory notes, and the prospectus asserted a 100% return of investment cash through immediate tax benefits and a tax write-off equalling 400% of the initial cash payment.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed the claimed IRC § 174 deductions in full and determined federal income tax deficiencies against the participating taxpayers, together with additions to tax under IRC § 6661 for substantial understatement of tax and IRC § 6653(a) for negligence, and the increased interest rate under IRC § 6621 on underpayments attributable to tax-motivated transactions. The disallowance rested on two legal grounds reflected in the Tax Court and Tenth Circuit opinions. First, applying the two-step "generic tax shelter" and "economic substance" test of Rose v. Commissioner, 88 T.C. 386 (1987), the Tax Court found that the AMR transactions lacked economic substance and that the taxpayers entered them for tax benefits only, and not for profit. Second, although the Tax Court did not focus on the question, the Tenth Circuit identified a "clearer and simpler basis" for denying the deductions: the expenditures were not paid or incurred "in connection with [the taxpayers'] trade or business" as mandated by IRC § 174(a)(1). Because the agreements did not obligate R & D Labs to do anything, provided no reporting or accounting to the purchasers, and conveyed no ownership rights in the underlying technology, the Tax Court's findings indicated that the taxpayers' activities never went beyond those of passive investors.
Governing Statutory Framework

The dispute centered on the statutory interpretation of IRC § 174(a)(1), which allows a taxpayer to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as deductible expenses, or, following the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act amendments to § 174, as specified research or experimental expenditures subject to mandatory capitalization and amortization; for domestic research or experimental expenditures in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21) restored immediate deductibility under new IRC § 174A, which likewise requires that the expenditures be paid or incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business, while foreign research remains subject to capitalization under § 174. Historically, the United States Supreme Court in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), held that Congress purposefully selected the broader phrase "in connection with his trade or business" in § 174—rather than the stricter phrase "in carrying on any trade or business" found in IRC § 162(a)—to encourage nascent enterprises and startups to conduct R&D prior to achieving commercial sales.

However, the Tax Court and federal appellate courts subsequently clarified that Snow did not abolish the trade or business requirement altogether or convert § 174 into a statutory vehicle for passive investors to deduct capital contributions. In evaluating whether an activity constitutes a bona fide business rather than a tax-avoidance mechanism or hobby, courts also integrate the profit-objective principles of IRC § 183 and Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b), alongside IRC § 165(c) and IRC § 212.

For contemporary R&D tax credit practitioners, Nickeson—although it addressed only the § 174 deduction for the 1982 tax year and did not consider the research credit—bears directly on IRC § 41 through two explicit statutory mechanisms. First, under the gateway test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), an activity cannot constitute "qualified research" unless the underlying expenditures are eligible to be treated as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, the amended provision requires that the expenditures be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A). Any legal or evidentiary failure under the Nickeson standard that disqualifies expenditures under § 174 automatically disqualifies those expenditures from the § 41 credit computation. Second, IRC § 41(b)(1) imposes an even stricter trade or business threshold by mandating that Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—including in-house wages, supplies, and 65% of eligible contract research expenses under § 41(b)(3)—must be paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer". Because "carrying on" under § 41(b)(1) is narrower than "in connection with" under § 174, a taxpayer that fails the Nickeson threshold for § 174 necessarily fails the trade or business requirement of § 41.
The Court's Final Holding

The United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's decision in Brock v. Commissioner, upholding the complete disallowance of the taxpayers' § 174 deductions, as well as the § 6661 and § 6653(a) additions to tax and the increased interest rate for tax-motivated transactions. Writing for the appellate panel, Judge Logan held that to establish that claimed § 174 expenses were incurred "in connection with their trade or business," taxpayers must show both a profit motive, which they bear the burden of proving, and that their activities were "substantial and regular enough to establish that they were actively involved in the trade or business" rather than merely passive investment.

Reviewing the Tax Court's factual findings under the "clearly erroneous" standard and its application of the law to those facts de novo, the Tenth Circuit concluded that the record supported the Tax Court's findings, which reflected the characteristics courts commonly rely on in rejecting deductions for lack of profit motive—specifically, marketing on the basis of projected tax benefits, a grossly inflated purchase price set without bargaining, the taxpayers' failure to inquire into potential profitability, their lack of control over the activities, and the use of nonrecourse indebtedness. The Tenth Circuit upheld the Tax Court's determination that the taxpayers had not met their burden of showing a good-faith intent to profit and that the AMR purchase agreement was "the naked sale of tax benefits".
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the research claims in Nickeson v. Commissioner stemmed from cascading legal, financial, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies. Rather than failing on a narrow technicality, the taxpayers' claims collapsed because the underlying legal and economic architecture contradicted the statutory purpose of IRC § 174 and, by extension, the IRC § 41 framework that incorporates it.
Absence of an Objective Profit Motive and the Five Nickeson Factors

A foundational prerequisite for claiming deductions under IRC § 174 or credits under IRC § 41 is that the taxpayer must engage in the underlying research venture with the predominant, good-faith objective of earning an economic profit independent of federal tax savings. While the inquiry into profit motive involves subjective intent, the Tenth Circuit explained that objective evidence may be used to establish that intent and that, although the § 183 factors are helpful, they are not exclusive, because "all of the unique circumstances of a case must be considered"; the § 183 regulations similarly direct that greater weight be given to objective facts than to the taxpayer's mere statement of intent (Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(a)). Alongside the nine nonexclusive factors of Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b), the Tenth Circuit in Nickeson, drawing on a review of prior R&D and related cases, identified a non-exhaustive ("inter alia") list of five characteristics that courts rely on in rejecting deductions for lack of profit motive—characteristics the Tenth Circuit has since applied as the five Nickeson signs that a taxpayer lacks a profit motive, for example in Olsen v. Commissioner (10th Cir. 2022).

The first deficiency was marketing focused on projected tax benefits. The offering documents emphasized the tax benefits of the transaction: the prospectus asserted a 100% return of investment cash through immediate tax benefits and a tax write-off equalling 400% of the initial cash payment, and the purchase agreement emphasized tax benefits rather than profit potential. When promotional materials demonstrate that an investor recovers their initial cash outlay purely through tax reductions regardless of whether the technology ever functions commercially, courts infer that the transaction is an abusive tax shelter.

The second deficiency was the presence of grossly inflated purchase prices set without arm's-length bargaining. The taxpayers accepted the demanded purchase price for the AMR components without negotiation, and the Tax Court found that price "illusory and far in excess of the actual value," with the cost of producing the components only a fraction of the stated purchase price. In a genuine commercial R&D transaction, a business principal negotiates to minimize development costs and maximize return on invested capital. The willingness of the Nickeson taxpayers to accept the demanded, overstated purchase price without bargaining supported the Tax Court's finding that they entered the AMR transaction for tax benefits only, and not for profit.

The third deficiency involved the taxpayers' failure to inquire into potential profitability. The Tax Court found that the taxpayers had no independent appraisal of the AMR components and relied instead on the information in the promoter's prospectus. They did not independently verify the financial and technical assumptions provided by the promoters, even though the purchase agreements did not describe the research needed to develop the AMR to a marketable state.

The fourth deficiency was the taxpayers' complete lack of control over research activities. The purchase agreement had no provision for reporting to purchasers on the progress of research, no time schedule for the research, and no agreement for accounting to the taxpayers on progress or expenditures of funds, and the Tax Court found the agreement vague to the point of being illusory, with R & D Labs not obligated to do anything. Whether and how any research was performed thus remained within the control of the promoter and his affiliated R & D Labs rather than the taxpayers.

The fifth deficiency centered on the reliance on nonrecourse or contingent debt. The deferred promissory notes, which constituted 75% of the purchase price, were payable from and secured by the proceeds of exploiting the information generated by the research and were nonrecourse in substance; because Risk testified that no information was to be provided to investors until the notes were paid off, the court observed that, as the government argued, the arrangement suggested the notes probably were not enforceable. Although the Tax Court found the notes lacking in commercial value, the taxpayers' claimed deductions included their full face amount, so the notes served chiefly to multiply the claimed § 174 expenditure figures.
Failure to Satisfy the Trade or Business Requirement: Passivity vs. Substantial and Regular Activity

Beyond the lack of profit motive, the Tenth Circuit articulated a strict bilateral test for the statutory "trade or business" nexus under IRC § 174, holding that to establish that claimed § 174 expenses were in connection with their trade or business, taxpayers must show both a profit motive and that their activities were substantial and regular enough to establish that they were actively involved in the trade or business.

In Nickeson and subsequent Tenth Circuit jurisprudence—such as LDL Research & Development II, Ltd. v. Commissioner, 124 F.3d 1338 (10th Cir. 1997), where a limited partnership paid Larson-Davis Laboratories to develop electronic acoustic and vibration testing equipment—the courts drew a sharp boundary between active business operations and passive capital management. Consistent with Higgins v. Commissioner, 312 U.S. 212 (1941), which Nickeson cites, managing one's own investments, however time-consuming, does not by itself constitute a trade or business, even where research is actually performed by a third party. The taxpayers in Nickeson failed this requirement because, as the Tenth Circuit observed, the Tax Court's findings indicated that their activities never went beyond those of passive investors: they paid cash, executed deferred notes, and received no reports or accounting on the progress of research or the expenditure of funds. Nothing in the findings indicated that the taxpayers, who purchased component interests individually, directed the research or carried on any manufacturing, marketing, or other operational activity of their own.
Contractual Divestiture of Commercialization Rights and Lack of Realistic Prospect

A critical contractual failure in Nickeson and related R&D limited partnership cases involved the allocation of intellectual property (IP) and commercialization rights. Although Nickeson itself rested on the passive-investor finding and did not apply a separate "realistic prospect" test, other appellate decisions—including the Tenth Circuit in LDL Research & Development II and the Fourth Circuit in Lewin v. Commissioner, 335 F.3d 345 (4th Cir. 2003)—hold that, to establish that outsourced R&D is incurred in connection with a taxpayer's trade or business, the taxpayer must demonstrate a "realistic prospect" of entering a trade or business to exploit the developed technology itself.

In Nickeson, the purchase agreements gave the taxpayers the right to technological information concerning the component purchased, or possibly the AMR as a whole, so that ostensibly they could manufacture and sell their component or sell the information to a licensee corporation created as part of the AMR project. The court found it significant, however, that the agreements did not transfer ownership rights in the underlying technology, which was patented by Harris Corporation and held by Risk only under a nonexclusive license he could not sublicense; the Tax Court also found the licensee arrangement questionable, and Risk testified that no information was to be provided to investors until the notes were paid off. By leaving the taxpayers without ownership of the technology and dependent on a promoter-created licensee arrangement and a prospective "royalty opportunity," the agreements were consistent with the court's conclusion that the taxpayers were passive investors rather than participants in an active trade or business; in other R&D partnership cases, such as LDL Research & Development II and Lewin, the same result followed from contractor purchase, licensing, or buyout options that left the partnership with no realistic prospect of exploiting the technology in its own business.
Direct Spillover Disqualifications Under IRC Section 41 (R&D Tax Credit)

When analyzed through the lens of modern federal R&D tax credit examinations, the contractual and evidentiary failures identified in Nickeson—a case decided under § 174 alone—would trigger four distinct statutory disqualifications under IRC § 41. First, the expenditures fail the IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) Section 174 eligibility test; because the expenditures cannot be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under § 174 due to lack of profit motive and trade or business nexus, they fail the first prong of the Four-Part Test. Second, the structure violates the IRC § 41(b)(1) "carrying on" requirement, which demands that a taxpayer claiming contract research expenses under § 41(b)(3) be presently carrying on an active trade or business to which the research relates, rather than merely holding technology for passive licensing or royalty collection.

Third, the arrangements fail under the contract research and funded research rules of IRC § 41(b)(3), IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). To claim 65% of payments to a third-party contractor as QREs, the contract must be executed prior to the performance of the qualified research, must specify that the research is performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and must require the taxpayer to bear the unconditional financial risk of failure while retaining substantial rights in the research results. In Nickeson-style structures, the use of nonrecourse or contingent debt meant the taxpayer did not bear genuine financial risk of technical failure, while the absence of any transfer of ownership rights in the underlying technology (and, in other R&D partnership cases, contractor purchase options) divested the taxpayer of substantial rights. Fourth, although Nickeson did not decide any substantiation or process-of-experimentation question—the court stressed that the issue was the taxpayers' intent, not whether any research was performed or its value—the record showed purchase agreements with no description of the research needed, no time frame, and no accounting on progress or expenditures, together with testimony that very little research was actually done on the AMR, so a taxpayer in that position could not produce technical records showing how it identified technological uncertainty, formulated hypotheses, or conducted a structured process of experimentation under § 41(d)(1)(C), nor substantiate how lump-sum, unnegotiated purchase prices corresponded to actual qualified engineering hours or supplies.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial requirement addressed in Nickeson v. Commissioner (and its integrated IRC §§ 174 and 41 framework) against the specific taxpayer failures identified in the ruling and the court's governing standard of proof.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Mandate

cells: Bona Fide Objective Profit Motive

Entered the AMR transaction for tax benefits only, and not for profit; relied on a prospectus asserting a 100% return of investment cash via tax benefits and a 400% write-off, and the Tax Court characterized the purchase agreement as "the naked sale of tax benefits".

Taxpayer bears the burden of showing that the activity was undertaken in good faith with the dominant hope and intent of realizing a profit; although the inquiry concerns subjective intent, objective evidence may be used to establish it, and the § 183 factors are helpful but not exclusive.
Arm's-Length Valuation & Economic Substance
Nickeson, 962 F.2d at 977; IRC §§ 174, 6700(b)(1)(A) (valuation overstatement context).

Accepted the demanded purchase price for the AMR components without negotiation or independent appraisal; the Tax Court found the price "illusory and far in excess of the actual value" and the cost of producing the components a fraction of the stated price.

The court did not prescribe a pricing-documentation standard; it treated a grossly inflated purchase price set without bargaining as objective evidence of a missing profit motive. Itemized engineering budgets, third-party quotes, or independent cost valuations are prudent practice for showing arm's-length pricing.
Genuine Financial Risk & Bona Fide Indebtedness
Nickeson, 962 F.2d at 977; IRC §§ 174(a), 465; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2).

Financed 75% of the purchase price with deferred promissory notes payable from and secured by the proceeds of exploiting the research information, which were nonrecourse in substance, lacking in commercial value, and probably not enforceable.

Nickeson treats the use of nonrecourse indebtedness as a sign of a missing profit motive; for § 41 contract research, the regulations separately require that payments be incurred at the taxpayer's financial risk under an agreement entered into prior to the performance of the research.
Pre-Investment & Ongoing Commercial Inquiry
Nickeson, 962 F.2d at 977; Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b)(1)–(3).
Had no independent appraisal of the AMR components and relied on the information in the promoter's prospectus, although the agreements did not describe the research needed or set a time frame for it.

Failure to inquire into potential profitability weighs against a profit motive; because the expertise of the taxpayer or his advisors is one of the § 183 factors, contemporaneous independent feasibility reviews, business plans, and market analyses by advisors independent of the promoter are prudent evidence rather than an express judicial mandate.
Active Control Over Research Activities
Nickeson, 962 F.2d at 977–78; Brock, T.C. Memo. 1989-641.

Agreement had no provision for progress reports, no time schedule, and no accounting on expenditures; it was vague to the point of being illusory, and R & D Labs, a promoter affiliate, was not obligated to do anything.

Lack of control over activities weighs against a profit motive and indicates that taxpayers were at most passive investors; regular design reviews, milestone approval gates, change-order authority, and active management personnel are practical ways to evidence control.
"Substantial and Regular" Trade or Business Nexus
Acted solely as passive investors who paid cash and executed deferred notes; the Tax Court's findings indicated their activities never went beyond those of passive investors.
Taxpayer must prove both a profit motive and "substantial and regular" operational activities establishing active engagement in a trade or business, not mere passive investment or royalty collection.
Realistic Prospect of Commercial Exploitation & IP Retention
Nickeson, 962 F.2d at 975, 977–78; LDL Research & Development II, 124 F.3d 1338; IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(3).

Acquired only a right to technological information, with no transfer of ownership rights in the underlying technology (patented by Harris Corporation and licensed to the promoter nonexclusively); the licensee arrangement was questionable, and information was to be withheld until the notes were paid off.

Under later § 174 decisions, the taxpayer must show a realistic prospect of exploiting the technology in its own trade or business; for § 41, the taxpayer must retain substantial rights in the developed technology and maintain a realistic operational capability and business plan to manufacture, sell, lease, or use the resulting business component in its own active trade or business.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To illustrate how contemporary corporate taxpayers, joint ventures, and tax advisors must structure R&D arrangements to survive IRS scrutiny under Nickeson v. Commissioner, the following two industry case studies examine realistic commercial projects initially compromised by the exact legal pitfalls identified by the Tenth Circuit. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remediation blueprint across project governance, contract architecture, financial risk allocation, and technical documentation.
Case Study 1: Acoustic & Vibration Instrumentation Joint Venture (Outsourced Hardware & Firmware R&D)
Initial Defective Project Profile and Nickeson Pitfalls

Apex Industrial Holdings, LLC ("Apex"), a U.S. mid-market industrial group formed by high-net-worth engineering executives, seeks to develop a next-generation multi-channel acoustic and structural vibration analyzer—utilizing real-time octave band analysis and ultra-low-noise piezoresistive transducers—for aerospace and mass-timber structural testing. Rather than conducting the R&D internally, Apex forms a special-purpose limited partnership, Apex Acoustic R&D LP ("the Partnership"), which enters into a turnkey Research and Development Agreement with VibraTech Labs, Inc. ("VibraTech"), an established acoustic instrumentation manufacturer.

Under the initial defective structure, the Partnership agrees to pay VibraTech a lump-sum fee of $6,000,000 in Year 1. The Partnership funds $1,200,000 in cash—raised from partners following an offering memorandum that heavily highlights immediate IRC § 174 deductions and IRC § 41 R&D tax credits—and executes a $4,800,000 nonrecourse promissory note payable over 10 years solely out of 12% of future net sales of the acoustic analyzer. The price of $6,000,000 was proposed unilaterally by VibraTech's founder without an itemized engineering budget or price negotiation. Furthermore, the contract grants VibraTech complete discretion over all engineering specifications and includes a Technology Option Agreement allowing VibraTech to acquire an exclusive worldwide license to manufacture and sell the completed acoustic analyzer in exchange for a 5% passive royalty payable to the Partnership.

This structure fails comprehensively under Nickeson and IRC §§ 174 and 41. First, all five Nickeson tax-shelter factors are present: the offering materials focus on projected tax benefits, the $6,000,000 fee is unnegotiated and unsupported by an independent cost breakdown, the partners conducted no independent commercial feasibility inquiry, the Partnership exercises zero control over VibraTech's day-to-day R&D, and 80% of the contract is financed via a contingent, nonrecourse note. Second, the venture lacks "substantial and regular" business activity and a realistic prospect of entering a trade or business; because the Partnership has no employees, no manufacturing or sales operations, and granted VibraTech an exclusive option that relegates the Partnership to passive royalty collection, the Partnership is merely a passive investment conduit. Third, the contract research QREs are disqualified under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e) because the $4,800,000 contingent note insulates the Partnership from the unconditional financial risk of failure for that portion, while the exclusive license option divests the Partnership of substantial rights in the research results.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint

To transform this arrangement into a compliant, audit-ready R&D structure that satisfies Nickeson, IRC § 174, and IRC § 41, tax counsel must execute a four-phase remediation prior to the commencement of research activities.
Step 1: Corporate Governance & Active Trade or Business Integration

Instead of isolating the R&D inside a passive, standalone limited partnership marketed for tax write-offs, Apex must fold the project directly into an active operating subsidiary—Apex Instrumentation Systems, Inc. ("Apex Operating")—or restructure the Partnership into an active operating joint venture where Apex personnel conduct substantial and regular commercial and technical operations. Apex Operating must assign internal technical and commercial staff to the project, including a Lead Acoustic Systems Architect, a Firmware Integration Manager, and a Director of Commercial Sales, thereby establishing an active operational infrastructure. To overcome the Nickeson lack-of-control defect, Apex Operating must institute a mandatory bi-weekly Technical Steering Committee (TSC) recorded via contemporaneous formal minutes, granting Apex Operating's Lead Architect binding contractual authority to approve circuit schematics, review digital signal processing (DSP) algorithms, direct prototype rework, and authorize milestone disbursements. Simultaneously, management must scrub all internal capital-raising memoranda and board presentations of tax-shelter promotion, replacing them with a comprehensive pre-tax commercial business plan prepared by an independent acoustic industry consultant that documents projected unit manufacturing costs, bill of materials (BOM) targets, ASTM/ISO acoustic compliance standards such as ASTM E1007-16 impact sound measurement protocols, and five-year pre-tax discounted cash flow (DCF) models proving a compelling pre-tax return on investment.
Step 2: Financial Risk Restructuring & Arm's-Length Valuation

To eliminate the Nickeson valuation overstatement and nonrecourse debt pitfalls, the financial terms of the VibraTech contract must be completely overhauled. Apex Operating must obtain competitive engineering proposals from at least two alternative acoustic contract engineering firms or commission an independent third-party engineering cost appraisal, negotiating the contract fee at arm's length to reduce the bloated $6,000,000 figure to its true fair market engineering cost of $2,150,000. This negotiated fee must be backed by a granular Statement of Work (SOW) breaking down hourly engineering rates by discipline—across acoustic physics, printed circuit board (PCB) layout, FPGA firmware, and environmental testing—alongside prototype material supplies. Furthermore, the parties must abolish the $4,800,000 nonrecourse promissory note entirely, funding the $2,150,000 contract exclusively through at-risk equity capital contributions and, if debt is utilized, full-recourse commercial bank financing secured by Apex Operating's balance sheet. Finally, payments under the Master Services Agreement (MSA) must be structured on a pure Time-and-Materials (T&M) basis or around fixed-price technical review gates where payment is unconditionally owed for engineering hours expended regardless of whether the acoustic transducer achieves its target signal-to-noise ratio, proving that Apex Operating bears 100% of the financial risk of technical failure under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2).
Step 3: Contractual Re-Engineering of Intellectual Property & Commercialization Rights

To satisfy the "realistic prospect of entering a trade or business" standard applied in post-Nickeson decisions such as LDL Research & Development II and the IRC § 41 "substantial rights" requirement, the Technology Option Agreement must be formally rescinded. Apex Operating and VibraTech must execute an amended MSA stipulating that 100% of all foreground intellectual property, patents, trade secrets, CAD layouts, and DSP source code vest exclusively in Apex Operating upon creation via present assignment of future inventions, with no purchase option or exclusive buyout right granted to VibraTech. Additionally, Apex Operating must document a concrete operational pathway to commercialize the analyzer directly in its own trade or business. If VibraTech is subsequently retained to assemble commercial units, the parties must execute a separate Contract Manufacturing Agreement (CMA) under which VibraTech acts strictly as a toll manufacturer producing units to Apex's specifications for a fixed per-unit assembly fee, while Apex Operating retains legal title to all inventory, manages customer warranty obligations, and sells the analyzers under the Apex brand through its own direct sales force.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation & Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d) and substantiate the 65% contract research QREs under § 41(b)(3) alongside internal supervisory wages, Apex Operating must institute strict technical documentation protocols. Prior to each development sprint, Apex's Lead Architect and VibraTech's lead engineer must document the specific technological uncertainties—such as eliminating low-frequency thermal noise distortion across octave bands between 20 Hz and 200 Hz while maintaining a dynamic range exceeding 120 dB—and the competing design hypotheses formulated to resolve them. Throughout execution, the teams must maintain a centralized digital repository containing finite element analysis (FEA) acoustic simulations, reverberation room test logs, prototype failure reports, and firmware version-control commits. Finally, Apex Operating must contractually require VibraTech to submit monthly invoices that cross-reference each billed engineering hour to a specific SOW research task and uncertainty identifier, explicitly segregating qualified experimentation hours from excluded post-production, routine quality control, or commercial tooling activities.
Case Study 2: Solar Thermal Concentrator & Molten-Salt Heat Transfer Syndicate (Pilot Model & Equipment Development)
Initial Defective Project Profile and Nickeson Pitfalls

Helios Industrial Partners ("Helios"), a consortium of U.S. manufacturing corporations and individual executives, seeks to claim IRC § 174 R&E deductions, IRC § 41 R&D tax credits (claiming pilot model supply QREs), and IRC §§ 167 and 168 depreciation deductions on a project to develop modular parabolic solar thermal concentrator arrays ("lenses/collectors") coupled with a closed-loop molten-salt heat exchanger for industrial process heat. Helios enters into a Turnkey Development and Equipment Purchase Agreement with Solaris Energy Corp. ("SolArix"). Under the promotional package distributed by SolArix, Helios agrees to purchase and fund the development of 200 prototype concentrator lens assemblies at a stated price of $15,000 per assembly ($3,000,000 total).

Helios pays a 30% cash down payment ($900,000) upon signing, while the remaining 70% ($2,100,000) is financed via a long-term nonrecourse installment obligation payable only beginning five years after the concentrator arrays begin generating commercial electricity revenue. Simultaneously, Helios leases the prototype assemblies back to a SolArix affiliate ("SolArix Operations, LLC"), which promises to assemble, test, and operate the arrays on test towers and pay Helios a fixed annual lease fee once commercial power generation begins. In reality, raw uncut polymer and glass sheets costing $400 per unit sit unmounted in a warehouse, SolArix has not finalized whether the heat transfer fluid will be water, synthetic oil, or molten salt, and Helios personnel never visit the site or direct any engineering. Nevertheless, Helios claims the full $3,000,000 basis for R&D pilot model supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2) and § 174, alongside depreciation deductions.

This structure fails directly under the Nickeson precedent, as specifically applied by the Tenth Circuit to solar energy shelters in United States v. RaPower-3, LLC and Olsen v. Commissioner. First, the transaction is marketed around zeroing out federal tax liability via the 30% cash outlay, the $15,000 unit price represents a gross valuation overstatement (37.5 times the $400 raw material cost) accepted without bargaining, the 70% balance is illusory contingent and nonrecourse debt, and Helios exercises zero operational control. Second, the claim violates the statutory exclusion of depreciable property from R&D supplies and fails the pilot model rules. Under IRC § 174(c) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation cannot be claimed as qualified research supplies. Furthermore, because the uncut sheets sit idle in a warehouse and are neither placed in service in an active trade or business nor subjected to a structured process of experimentation as a qualified "pilot model" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), both the R&D tax credit and depreciation claims are wholly invalid.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint

To pursue legitimate solar thermal concentrator and heat-transfer R&D that satisfies the Tenth Circuit's Nickeson mandate and the strict requirements of IRC §§ 174 and 41, the taxpayer must dismantle the sale-leaseback shelter and rebuild the project as an authentic engineering development program.
Step 1: Dismantling the Passive Leaseback & Establishing an Active Engineering Entity

Helios must immediately terminate the passive equipment purchase and leaseback structure with SolArix. Instead, the industrial sponsors must form an active operating corporation or substantive joint venture—Helios Thermal Engineering, Inc. ("HTE")—staffed with qualified mechanical, chemical, and thermal engineers. HTE must lease or construct a dedicated solar thermal test facility, or lease a dedicated experimental test bay at a national laboratory or university research park, operated under HTE's direct managerial control. To satisfy the "substantial and regular" activity test of Nickeson, HTE's internal engineering team must directly author the thermal system architecture, perform optical ray-tracing simulations, manage material procurement, and physically supervise test-tower assembly and fluid-loop testing. Prior to capital commitment, HTE must also commission an independent levelized cost of heat (LCOH) and levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) engineering-economic feasibility study demonstrating how the proposed parabolic concentrator and molten-salt loop can achieve commercial profitability against natural gas industrial boilers without relying on federal tax credits or deductions to recover invested principal.
Step 2: Purging Valuation Overstatements, Nonrecourse Debt & Improper Capitalization

To cure the financial and statutory categorization defects under Nickeson, IRC § 174(c), and IRC § 41(b)(2), HTE must eliminate all promoter markups and contingent financing. Instead of purchasing "lenses" from a promoter at an inflated $15,000 unit price financed by 70% contingent debt, HTE must procure raw materials, optical-grade polymer films, structural aluminum frames, and molten-salt valves directly from third-party industrial vendors at actual arm's-length market prices (e.g., $400 to $850 per assembly component), paid 100% in cash or full-recourse working capital.

Simultaneously, tax counsel must enforce a strict accounting segregation between depreciable capital assets and consumable pilot models under IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Permanent test-facility infrastructure—such as permanent steel support towers, concrete foundations, and multi-year diagnostic instrumentation—must be capitalized as depreciable property under IRC § 168, placed in service only when physically erected and operational, and strictly excluded from IRC § 41 supply QREs. Conversely, for the experimental concentrator assemblies and sacrificial heat-exchanger tubes to qualify as non-depreciable R&D supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2) and § 174, HTE must construct only the specific number of experimental prototype assemblies (such as 6 to 12 full-scale experimental collector modules rather than 200 warehouse units) strictly necessary to test and resolve technical design uncertainties. HTE must contemporaneously document that these prototype modules are consumed, destroyed in thermal stress testing, or scrapped after experimental validation rather than held for commercial leasing or power generation.
Step 3: Re-Architecting Third-Party Fabrication & Engineering Contracts

Where HTE engages external specialists—such as an optical coating laboratory or a high-temperature metallurgy contractor—HTE must execute distinct, pre-performance R&D subcontracts compliant with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). Under these agreements, HTE must specify the exact technical parameters, retain 100% of all intellectual property and patent rights, and pay for engineering and fabrication services on a fixed-hourly or non-contingent milestone basis. Furthermore, to prevent the warehouse-inventory disqualification highlighted in RaPower-3 and Olsen, HTE must maintain bills of lading, serial-number tracking logs, and timestamped engineering commissioning records proving that every fabricated component is delivered to the test site, physically mounted onto the experimental test loop, and actively subjected to thermal testing during the taxable year for which the expenditure is claimed.
Step 4: Structuring the Process of Experimentation & Contemporaneous Substantiation

To satisfy the Four-Part Test under IRC § 41(d)—including the "substantially all" (80%) process of experimentation threshold of § 41(d)(1)(C)—and avoid disallowance under the pilot-model and substantiation standards applied in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner and Betz v. Commissioner, HTE must track its engineering activities at the granular business-component level. HTE should formally define each discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)—for example, designating the Parabolic Polymer-Composite Concentrator Mirror Assembly as Business Component 1 and the Eutectic Nitrate Molten-Salt Receiver Tube Header as Business Component 2—and apply the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) where necessary. For each component, HTE engineers must document the exact capability and design uncertainties, such as preventing delamination of reflective silvered polymer films under concentrated ultraviolet flux and mitigating thermal-cycling fatigue in receiver welds operating between 290°C and 565°C.

HTE must then record the structured process of experimentation executed for each pilot module, encompassing optical computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and thermal stress modeling, fabrication of competing mirror substrate geometries and molten-salt alloy receiver configurations, empirical on-sun thermal efficiency and accelerated lifecycle testing, and quantitative evaluation of heat-transfer coefficients and focal degradation. Finally, HTE must implement project-level enterprise resource planning (ERP) job-costing codes that link every engineer's daily timesheet, every material purchase order, and every third-party testing invoice directly to the specific experimental test protocol and business component, establishing a comprehensive evidentiary trail for IRS examination.
5. Synthesis of Remedial Governance vs. Defective Nickeson Structures

The following table synthesizes the operational, contractual, and evidentiary transformations required across both case studies to convert a defective structure into a fully compliant federal R&D tax position.

cells: Entity & Operational Role
Passive individual investors (as in Nickeson), or a passive limited partnership or investor syndicate, with no technical staff, facilities, or day-to-day operational involvement.
Active operating corporation or substantive joint venture employing technical leads who conduct "substantial and regular" R&D governance and commercialization.
Promotional & Financial Intent
Offering memoranda emphasize first-year tax write-offs exceeding cash invested ("naked sale of tax benefits").
Independent pre-tax commercial business plan, market feasibility analysis, and DCF models proving a primary pre-tax profit motive.
Pricing & Capitalization
Unnegotiated, grossly inflated lump-sum fees financed 70%–80% by nonrecourse or revenue-contingent promissory notes.
Arm's-length, competitively bid T&M or itemized engineering budgets funded 100% by at-risk equity or full-recourse commercial capital.
IP Rights & Exploitation Prospect

Taxpayer receives no ownership rights in the underlying technology (as in Nickeson), or the contractor holds an exclusive buyout or licensing option (as in LDL Research & Development II and Lewin); taxpayer relegated to a passive royalty prospect with no realistic prospect of business entry.
Taxpayer retains 100% unencumbered ownership ("substantial rights") of all foreground IP and executes a direct manufacturing/sales operational plan.
Physical Asset & Supply Treatment
Unmounted raw materials stored in warehouses claimed as depreciable assets and R&D supplies simultaneously.
Strict segregation of IRC § 168 depreciable test infrastructure from Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) non-depreciable pilot models actively consumed in testing.
Technical Substantiation
Lump-sum invoices lacking technical detail; no records of taxpayer technical supervision or iterative experimentation.
Contemporaneous TSC minutes, uncertainty/hypothesis logs, empirical test data, and ERP job-costing tying hours and supplies to specific business components.
